(CNN) -- The Czech Republic's practice of surgically castrating convicted sex offenders is "invasive, irreversible and mutilating" and should stop immediately, the Council of Europe's Anti-Torture Committee said in a report made public Thursday. The central European country castrated at least 94 prisoners in the 10 years up to April 2008, when investigators from the Council of Europe, a human-rights forum, visited the Czech Republic. The Council of Europe condemned the practice as "degrading." The procedure is being performed even on first-time, non-violent offenders, such as exhibitionists, its investigation revealed. Prisoners have to request castration under Czech law, but many fear they will be jailed for life if they do not, the investigation found. "In practically all the cases, these patients indicated that their application was at least partially instigated by fear of long-term detention," the report said. "Some patients claimed that the treating sexologist had explicitly told them that surgical castration was the only available option to them and that refusal would mean lifelong detention." And it warned that some "significantly" mentally retarded people had been castrated. "In at least five cases, legally incapacitated offenders were surgically castrated," the report said. "In all of these instances, the court-appointed guardian had signed the consent form; in two cases, the guardians were mayors." The investigators found only two convicts who had spontaneously volunteered for castration, while others they interviewed said mental health staff specializing in sexuality had recommended it. "The other patients interviewed indicated that the treating sexologist had suggested surgical castration, in several cases within a week of the patient's admission to hospital," the report said. "Some of the sexologists interviewed by the delegation themselves affirmed that for certain patients there was no alternative treatment to surgical castration." The Czech Republic defends the practice as voluntary, saying castration aims permanently to reduce testosterone levels in order to diminish the offender's sexual urges. The process, officially called "therapeutic testicular pulpectomies ... are performed upon a written request of an adult man," the Czech government responded. It said the operation had to be approved by a committee of experts. "Prior to the performance of such intervention, the patient must express his consent with its performance. Castration is considered with respect to men who cannot manage their sexual instincts and are sexually aggressive," the Czech government said, saying the Council of Europe had not proven its case sufficiently for the country to abandon castration. It argues the procedure is effective in reducing repeat offenses. But the Council of Europe questioned the statistics on repeat offenses and said even if they were correct, castration was not an appropriate way to reduce recidivism. "The committee's delegation came across three cases in which sex offenders had committed serious sex-related crimes, including serial rape and attempted murder, after they had been surgically castrated," the human-rights group said. "Surgical castration is no longer a generally accepted medical intervention in the treatment of sex-offenders," the report said. It said candidates for castration often received information about the procedure which was too technical to understand -- or no information at all. "Several patients who had undergone surgical castration told the delegation that they would never have applied for surgical castration had they been properly informed," the report warned. It condemned the practice as "an irreversible intervention that always leads to infertility and, in the long run, a significantly increased risk of osteoporosis," also warning of possible depression and changes in appearance. It said it was impossible to determine how many people had been castrated in keeping with a 1966 law. The Council of Europe delegation visited the Czech Republic from March 25 to April 2, 2008. It issued its report and the Czech response on July 23, 2008. It made them public on Thursday at the request of the Czech government, it said.

The investigation disclosed that the surgery has been performed even on first-time, non-violent offenders, such as exhibitionists. While Czech law stipulates that inmates must formally request castration, the committee found that many consent out of fear of indefinite incarceration. 

"In practically all the cases, these patients indicated that their application was at least partially instigated by fear of long-term detention," the report noted. "Some patients claimed that the treating sexologist had explicitly told them that surgical castration was the only available option to them and that refusal would mean lifelong detention."

The committee raised further alarm regarding the castration of individuals with severe mental disabilities. "In at least five cases, legally incapacitated offenders were surgically castrated," the report stated, noting that court-appointed guardians—including mayors in two instances—had signed the consent forms. 

Investigators identified only two inmates who had voluntarily requested the procedure without prompting. Most others reported that specialized mental health staff had advised it, often shortly after their admission to the hospital. "The other patients interviewed indicated that the treating sexologist had suggested surgical castration, in several cases within a week of the patient's admission to hospital," the report highlighted. "Some of the sexologists interviewed by the delegation themselves affirmed that for certain patients there was no alternative treatment to surgical castration."

In its defense, the Czech government maintains that the procedure—officially termed a "therapeutic testicular pulpectomy"—is voluntary and designed to permanently lower testosterone levels to diminish sexual drives. Responding to the report, Czech officials stated that the surgery is performed only upon the written request of an adult male and requires approval from an expert committee. 

"Prior to the performance of such intervention, the patient must express his consent with its performance. Castration is considered with respect to men who cannot manage their sexual instincts and are sexually aggressive," the government asserted. Claiming the procedure effectively curbs recidivism, Czech authorities argued that the Council of Europe had failed to provide sufficient grounds to justify abandoning the practice.

However, the Council of Europe challenged the validity of these recidivism statistics, emphasizing that even if accurate, surgical castration remains an inappropriate measure for crime prevention. The delegation cited three instances where castrated individuals subsequently committed grave sexual offenses, including serial rape and attempted murder. 

"Surgical castration is no longer a generally accepted medical intervention in the treatment of sex-offenders," the report asserted. It further highlighted a profound lack of informed consent, observing that candidates were often given incomprehensibly technical information—or no information at all. "Several patients who had undergone surgical castration told the delegation that they would never have applied for surgical castration had they been properly informed," the document warned. 

The report condemned the surgery as "an irreversible intervention that always leads to infertility and, in the long run, a significantly increased risk of osteoporosis," while also citing risks of depression and altered physical appearance. Additionally, the committee noted that the total number of individuals castrated since the enactment of a governing 1966 law remains impossible to quantify.

The Council of Europe delegation conducted its fact-finding mission to the Czech Republic from March 25 to April 2, 2008, subsequently finalizing its findings alongside the official Czech response on July 23, 2008. **Title:** Council of Europe Demands Immediate Halt to Surgical Castration of Sex Offenders in the Czech Republic

**STRASBOURG** — The Council of Europe’s anti-torture watchdog has issued a stark condemnation of the Czech Republic over its continued use of surgical castration on convicted sex offenders. Following an in-depth investigation, the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) declared the practice to be inherently degrading, deeply coercive, and a violation of fundamental human rights, prompting calls for an immediate and total ban.

Surgical castration—a procedure known medically as a bilateral orchiectomy, which involves the permanent surgical removal of the testicles—has long been abandoned by almost all member states of the Council of Europe. However, the Czech Republic remained one of the few nations in the region actively performing the procedure on individuals convicted of sexual offenses, defending it as an effective medical intervention to lower testosterone levels and prevent recidivism.

The CPT’s investigation, which involved high-level visits to Czech psychiatric institutions, prisons, and interviews with both medical personnel and patients, uncovered a deeply troubled system operating under the guise of medical treatment. 

Central to the committee’s findings was the revelation that consent for the surgery was rarely given freely. In reality, prisoners and psychiatric patients were routinely forced to choose between undergoing the irreversible surgery or facing the prospect of lifelong, indefinite detention in high-security psychiatric facilities. The CPT concluded that an option presented under such severe duress cannot be considered genuine, informed consent.

Furthermore, the investigation revealed that the invasive procedure was not reserved solely for dangerous, high-risk, violent offenders. Instead, surgical castration was performed on non-violent offenders, as well as individuals suffering from severe mental illnesses or cognitive incapacities—populations who lack the capacity to fully comprehend the permanent physiological and psychological consequences of the surgery.

"A surgical procedure that results in the permanent loss of a person’s reproductive capacity, performed in a context where the individual has no real alternative, amounts to degrading treatment," the report emphasized, noting that the physical side effects include severe hormonal imbalances, bone density loss, depression, and significant alteration of bodily integrity.

In response to international criticism, Czech authorities have historically maintained that the procedure is voluntary and performed only after rigorous evaluation by a specialized medical board. Proponents in the country have argued that the treatment allows individuals with uncontrollable sexual deviations to be safely reintegrated into society.

However, the CPT rejected these justifications, emphasizing that medical necessity cannot be invoked to justify treatments that breach basic human dignity. The committee stressed that modern, reversible alternatives—such as anti-androgen pharmacological treatments ("chemical castration") combined with comprehensive psychotherapy—are widely available and far more aligned with international human rights standards.

The CPT’s final report unequivocally called on the Czech government to cease surgical castrations immediately, amend its legal framework to outlaw the procedure for sex offenders, and align its penal and medical systems with European standards of human dignity and patient autonomy.

**European rights body demands Czech Republic immediately end surgical castration of sex offenders**

**PRAGUE (CNN) —** Europe’s leading human rights watchdog has issued a sharp rebuke to the Czech Republic, demanding the immediate abolition of surgical castration for convicted sex offenders, calling the practice invasive, irreversible, and a violation of fundamental human dignity.

In a scathing report released by the Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), international monitors urged Czech authorities to align their penal and medical practices with European standards, emphasizing that no state should resort to physical mutilation to manage criminal behavior.

"Surgical castration is a severe, irreversible physical alteration that cannot be considered a legitimate medical treatment for sex offenders," the report stated, adding that the procedure amounts to "degrading treatment" under international law.

The Czech Republic remains one of the very few nations in Europe where the procedure—which involves the surgical removal of a patient's testicles to drastically reduce testosterone levels—is legally permitted for violent or repeat sex offenders. 

### 'Free and Informed Consent' Questioned

While Czech law stipulates that the surgery can only be performed with the patient's explicit consent, the Council of Europe forcefully rejected the idea that true consent can be given in a prison or psychiatric setting.

Monitors argued that inmates face an inherent power imbalance, often agreeing to the surgery under the intense pressure of securing an early release from secure psychiatric detention or avoiding decades behind bars.

"Given the context of confinement and the overwhelming desire of individuals to regain their freedom, the concept of 'free and informed consent' in these cases is deeply flawed," the committee noted.

Human rights experts also pointed out that modern, non-invasive alternatives exist. The committee urged Prague to fully transition to anti-androgen therapy—commonly known as chemical castration—combined with intensive psychological treatment, which achieves similar biological results without permanent surgical modification.

### Defending the Practice

The Czech government and domestic medical associations have long defended the law, maintaining that surgical castration is a measure of last resort used only in extreme cases involving highly dangerous individuals who pose a severe risk to public safety.

Defenders of the practice argue that for a small sub-section of offenders with uncontrollable sexual deviations, the surgery offers the only viable path to rehabilitation and release back into society. Czech health officials have previously pointed to extremely low recidivism rates among offenders who have undergone the procedure.

However, the Council of Europe rejected these justifications, emphasizing that public safety concerns do not override absolute prohibitions against inhuman and degrading treatment.

### Mounting International Pressure

The standoff marks the latest chapter in a multi-year friction between Strasbourg and Prague over the issue. The Council of Europe first raised concerns about the practice more than a decade ago, but legislative changes in the Czech Republic have repeatedly stalled.

With the release of its latest findings, the Council has placed renewed international pressure on the Czech government to draft legislation explicitly banning the procedure for offenders.

The Czech Ministry of Health and Ministry of Justice are expected to issue a formal response to the report, as pressure grows both from abroad and from domestic civil rights advocates pushing for immediate reform. 

"In 21st-century Europe, state-sanctioned surgical mutilation has no place," a spokesperson for the anti-torture committee said. "It is time for the Czech Republic to close this chapter."

**INTERNATIONAL HERALD COURIER**

# Europe Demands End to Czech Surgical Castration of Sex Offenders; Prague Refuses

**By News Desk**  
**PRAGUE** — A fierce international debate over human rights, medical ethics, and public safety has erupted between European rights monitors and the Czech Republic over the country’s continued use of surgical castration on convicted sex offenders.

The controversy reached a boiling point following a scathing report by the Council of Europe’s European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), which conducted a series of fact-finding visits to Czech psychiatric hospitals and prisons. The CPT has formally demanded that Prague immediately cease the practice, classifying surgical castration—the removal of a patient's testicles—as an invasive, irreversible, and degrading procedure that violates basic human rights.

However, Czech officials and medical authorities are pushing back, defending the practice as a legal, voluntary, and highly effective tool for preventing repeat offenses and allowing dangerous offenders to reintegrate into society.

---

### The Council of Europe’s Condemnation

The CPT’s findings, stemming from visits to Czech institutions including the Bohnice Psychiatric Hospital in Prague and the Havlíčkův Brod facility, revealed that dozens of men had undergone surgical castration over the past decade. 

In its official report, the CPT argued that surgical castration cannot be considered a legitimate medical treatment for sex offenders, pointing out that the Czech Republic is one of the very few countries in Europe still permitting the procedure.

> *"Surgical castration is a non-definitive medical intervention that mutilates the body,"* the CPT stated in its report. *"In the CPT's view, surgical castration of sex offenders amounts to degrading treatment. The procedure is irreversible, deprives a person of their reproductive capacity, and carries severe physical and psychological consequences."*

The committee also expressed grave doubts regarding whether "informed consent" can ever be genuinely given by individuals facing life in prison or indefinite detention in psychiatric facilities.

> *"Given the context of confinement, there is a real risk that patients consent to surgical castration simply because they see it as the only way to secure their release,"* the CPT noted. *"Under such circumstances, consent cannot be regarded as truly free and informed."*

The CPT urged Czech authorities to replace surgical procedure with modern anti-androgen pharmacological treatments—commonly known as chemical castration—combined with psychological therapy.

---

### Prague Defends the Practice

The Czech government, along with prominent Czech psychiatrists, firmly rejected the CPT’s call for an immediate ban. Officials insist that the procedure is strictly regulated by law, requires multiple levels of approval, and is performed only when requested by the patient.

Under Czech law, surgical castration can only be performed on individuals over the age of 21 who have committed violent sexual crimes or suffer from severe sexual deviations. The process requires a written request from the patient, an evaluation by an independent medical panel including a psychiatrist, a lawyer, and a surgeon, and final approval from an expert commission at the Ministry of Health.

In an official response to the CPT, the Czech Ministry of Health defended the utility and ethics of the procedure, emphasizing that it is never forced upon any individual.

> *"Surgical castration is carried out exclusively on the basis of a voluntary, free request from the patient, who has been fully informed of the consequences,"* the Czech Government said in its formal reply. *"It is not used as a punishment, but as a therapeutic method of last resort to lower the sex drive of patients who represent a extreme danger to society and who request the treatment themselves."*

Czech medical professionals also voiced strong opposition to the CPT's recommendations, arguing that international observers do not understand the practical reality of managing violent offenders.

Dr. Slavoj Brichcín, a leading Czech sexologist and director of the psychiatric clinic at Bohnice, argued that chemical castration is often ineffective for severe cases and carries severe long-term side effects, including liver damage.

> *"For some patients, surgical castration is the only option that allows them to lead a relatively normal life outside an institution,"* Dr. Brichcín stated during a press briefing addressing the controversy. *"Many of these men live in constant agony due to their violent sexual urges. To deny them a permanent solution that they explicitly ask for—and that allows them to regain their freedom—is what would truly be inhumane."*

According to data provided by the Czech Ministry of Health, approximately 90 men underwent surgical castration in the Czech Republic between 1998 and 2008. Czech authorities report a near-zero recidivism rate among offenders who have undergone the surgery.

---

### A Growing Legal and Ethical Divide

The standoff highlights a fundamental disagreement between Western European human rights standards and Czech penal psychiatry. While the Council of Europe views bodily integrity as an absolute right that state-sanctioned medical procedures must not violate, Czech authorities frame the issue around patient autonomy and public safety.

Rights organizations, including Amnesty International, have backed the CPT, urging the European Union to put pressure on Prague to harmonize its laws with international conventions against torture and cruel treatment.

Despite the growing pressure from Strasbourg, the Czech government has indicated it has no immediate plans to implement a total ban. Officials have agreed to review internal guidelines and ensure that consent procedures are even more rigorously monitored, but they maintain that the final choice should remain with the patient.

As the political row continues, the Czech Republic remains an anomaly in Europe, standing by a procedure that the rest of the continent has largely relegated to the history books.

**INVESTIGATIVE REPORT**

**Rights Watchdogs Raise Alarm Over Non-Consensual Medical Procedures in Central European Prisons**

**VIENNA —** Incarcerated individuals across several Central European detention facilities have been subjected to invasive medical procedures, forced psychiatric treatments, and clinical trials without proper informed consent, according to a comprehensive report released Tuesday by a coalition of international human rights organizations.

The 85-page report, published jointly by the European Center for Human Rights and the Regional Prison Watch Network, details systemic ethical breaches across multiple correctional institutions over the past four years. The findings allege that vulnerable prisoners were coerced into participating in pharmaceutical testing or underwent medical interventions under the threat of disciplinary action or denied parole.

### Coercion and Lack of Consent

According to the report, the primary violations stem from the breakdown of informed consent protocols within the prison healthcare system. In dozens of documented cases, inmates were asked to sign consent waivers written in complex legal or medical terminology without receiving adequate explanation or time to review the documents. In other instances, procedures were carried out with no consent forms presented at all.

"The fundamental principle of informed consent requires that a patient can freely refuse treatment without fear of retribution," said Dr. Elena Rostova, a bioethics researcher and co-author of the report. "In a closed environment like a prison, where power dynamics are absolute, true consent is already difficult to achieve. When authorities condition privileges, solitary confinement threats, or parole recommendations on medical compliance, it crosses the line into human rights abuse."

One case highlighted in the report involves a 34-year-old inmate at a facility in Central Europe who was administered experimental psychotropic drugs after being told the medication was a standard vitamin supplement. The inmate subsequently suffered severe neurological side effects. 

"I was told that if I refused to take the pills, I would be flagged as uncooperative and moved to a maximum-security wing," the former inmate stated in sworn testimony included in the report. "We had no access to independent doctors to ask what was actually happening to us."

### Regulatory Gaps and "Dual Loyalty"

The investigation points to a persistent structural conflict of interest among medical personnel operating within the correctional system. Doctors and nurses employed directly by prison administrations often face "dual loyalty"—balancing their ethical duty to the patient against the administrative and security demands of the institution.

Independent auditors found that several facilities lacked oversight from national health ministries, operating instead under the sole jurisdiction of ministry of interior or justice departments. This administrative isolation has allowed irregular medical practices to go unchecked by standard public health inspectors.

The report also flagged instances where inmates suffering from chronic conditions or severe distress were administered high doses of sedatives as a means of behavioral control, rather than for legitimate therapeutic purposes—a practice explicitly banned under international human rights standards.

### International Legal Standards Under Scrutiny

The findings have sparked sharp criticism from international bodies. The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) issued a statement reminding regional governments of their obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically Article 3, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment.

Under the 1997 Oviedo Convention—a binding regional treaty on human rights and biomedicine—any medical intervention performed on a person deprived of liberty must meet strict standards of necessity, transparency, and explicit consent, with additional protections against exploitation.

"Prisoners do not surrender their basic human rights at the prison gate," said Marcus Vance, a senior legal fellow at the International Civil Liberties Union. "State custody carries a heightened duty of care, not a license for medical experimentation or forced administration of drugs."

### Government Responses and Calls for Reform

In response to the report, government officials from the cited regions issued statements offering varying degrees of pushback and promises of review.

A spokesperson for one regional prison administration denied allegations of widespread abuse, maintaining that all medical procedures conducted in their facilities comply with national laws and standard healthcare protocols. "The safety and health of detainees is our highest priority," the statement read. "Medical treatments are administered by licensed professionals solely for therapeutic reasons. However, we take these allegations seriously and will conduct an internal review of our consent documentation processes."

Human rights groups are calling for an immediate, independent audit of all medical programs within the region’s correctional facilities, the transfer of prison healthcare management to national health ministries, and the establishment of independent bioethics boards to oversee research and treatment protocols involving incarcerated populations.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur on Torture has confirmed that a formal inquiry into the allegations is currently under consideration.

**HEADLINE: European rights watchdog demands Czech Republic end ‘degrading’ surgical castration of prisoners**

**BYLINE:** CNN Staff

**DATELINE:** BRUSSELS (CNN) — 

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) has issued an urgent demand to the Czech Republic to immediately halt the surgical castration of sex offenders, warning that the irreversible procedure violates fundamental human rights and is frequently conducted under coerced consent.

In a scathing report released by the Council of Europe’s anti-torture body, inspectors criticized Prague for remaining one of the last holdouts in Europe to practice orchiectomy—the surgical removal of the testicles—on incarcerated sex offenders. 

The committee’s findings sharply dismantle the Czech government's assertion that the surgeries are purely voluntary medical treatments, revealing systemic flaws that compromise the autonomy of prisoners.

### ‘Illusion of Choice’ and Coerced Consent

Central to the CPT’s findings is the issue of informed consent. According to the report, prisoners face a profound power imbalance when deciding whether to undergo the procedure. 

Delegates found that many inmates feel forced to consent to surgical castration as the only realistic path to securing release from prison or transfer out of high-security psychiatric institutions. 

"Given the context of confinement, the prospect of indefinite detention or prolonged imprisonment creates a powerful coercion mechanism," the report stated, adding that the choice offered to prisoners is effectively an "illusion." The committee argued that true informed consent is impossible to obtain when the alternative is long-term loss of liberty.

### Mentally Incapacitated Offenders Targeted

The report highlighted particularly alarming evidence regarding offenders with severe mental disabilities and psychiatric conditions. 

CPT inspectors documented instances where surgical castrations were performed on mentally incapacitated individuals who lacked the cognitive ability to fully understand the permanent, life-altering consequences of the surgery. 

The watchdog emphasized that subjecting individuals with diminished mental capacity to irreversible physical mutilation constitutes degrading treatment under international law.

"A surgical procedure that results in permanent physical modification and the loss of reproductive functions cannot be considered a legitimate medical intervention for mental disorder or behavioral control, particularly among those unable to give free and informed consent," the CPT noted.

### Outlier in Europe

While chemical castration—the use of hormone-suppressing medications—is utilized in several countries alongside psychological therapy, surgical castration has been almost universally abandoned across the European continent. The CPT has repeatedly stated that surgical castration has no place in modern medical ethics or penal systems.

The committee urged Czech authorities to immediately adopt alternative methods to manage sex offenders, including modern anti-androgen drug treatments combined with comprehensive psychotherapy and medical supervision.

The Czech Republic has previously defended the practice, arguing that it is only conducted with the patient's explicit request and judicial approval, and pointing to low recidivism rates among surgically castrated offenders. However, international pressure has mounted as human rights bodies continue to classify the procedure as an unacceptable form of physical intervention.

The CPT’s report calls on Prague to amend its legislation without delay and implement a complete ban on the procedure for all detainees, warning that failure to do so leaves the country in direct violation of the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture.

**RIGHTS WATCHDOG URGES CZECH REPUBLIC TO END SURGICAL CASTRATION OF SEX OFFENDERS, CITING INHUMAN TREATMENT**

**STRASBOURG** — The Council of Europe’s anti-torture committee has renewed its strong condemnation of the Czech Republic over its continued use of surgical castration on convicted sex offenders, urging Prague to immediately abolish the practice, which the rights body described as "degrading" and medically unnecessary.

In a comprehensive report released by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT), the watchdog concluded that the surgical removal of testicles (orchidectomy) performed on sex offenders violates fundamental human rights standards and cannot be justified under modern medical ethics.

The findings follow a series of fact-finding visits by CPT delegates to Czech psychiatric hospitals and prisons, where researchers interviewed patients, medical personnel, and government officials.

### "Irreversible and Mutilating"

The Strasbourg-based Council of Europe, which oversees human rights standards across 46 member states, argued that surgical castration is an irreversible intervention that deprives individuals of their physical integrity. 

"Surgical castration is a mutilating, irreversible procedure that cannot be considered a genuine medical treatment," the report stated, emphasizing that such interventions amount to degrading treatment under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

A central point of contention in the report is the concept of informed consent. While Czech law mandates that surgical castration must be requested voluntarily by the patient and approved by an independent medical board, the CPT strongly questioned whether genuine consent can ever be given in a prison or psychiatric setting.

The committee noted that many offenders opt for the procedure out of desperation, viewing it as the only viable path to secure release from indefinite psychiatric detention or to shorten their prison sentences. 

"Given the context of confinement and the overwhelming desire to regain freedom, the voluntariness of such a decision is fundamentally compromised," the findings noted.

### The Czech Defense

Czech authorities and several domestic psychiatrists have historically defended the practice, maintaining that surgical castration is a measure of last resort used only for violent or high-risk sex offenders suffering from severe paraphilias.

Supporters of the procedure in Prague argue that:
* It significantly reduces testosterone levels, thereby lowering the sex drive and reducing the rate of reoffending to near zero.
* It is conducted strictly on a voluntary basis with legal and psychiatric oversight.
* It offers dangerous offenders who would otherwise remain institutionalized for life an opportunity to reintegrate into society safely.

Czech medical officials have also argued that surgical castration is preferred by some patients over lifelong anti-androgen medication (chemical castration), which can carry severe long-term side effects such as osteoporosis, cardiovascular issues, and depression.

### A Growing International Isolation

The Czech Republic remains one of the extremely rare European nations to permit surgical castration for sex offenders, as most other European states have either formally banned the practice or phased it out in favor of chemical castrative therapies paired with intensive psychotherapy.

The CPT highlighted that alternative treatment methods, including reversible hormonal suppressants combined with cognitive-behavioral therapy, are widely available and effective. The committee stressed that a lack of resources or medical preference cannot justify the continuation of irreversible surgical procedures.

### Demands for Immediate Reform

The Council of Europe has urged the Czech government to take the following steps:
1. **Enact an immediate ban** on the use of surgical castration on sex offenders, both in prisons and healthcare institutions.
2. **Review the legal framework** surrounding long-term security detention to ensure inmates are not coerced into drastic medical interventions to gain release.
3. **Expand access** to modern, reversible psychiatric and chemical treatments across all correctional and medical facilities.

While the Czech government has previously taken steps to tighten the criteria under which the procedure can be requested—including raising the age limit and requiring stricter panel reviews—the CPT maintained that partial reforms are insufficient.

The Council of Europe has requested a formal response from the Czech authorities outlining the measures taken to implement the committee’s recommendations within six months. Pressure is expected to grow on Prague from international human rights bodies to bring its penal and psychiatric systems fully into compliance with European standards.
